content: The direction of the gravitational force per unit mass at a given point is aligned with what is commonly referred to as the vertical direction. However, the term vertical, while frequently used in everyday language, is often misunderstood or misapplied. A precise definition and further discussion are necessary to address these misconceptions. In the vicinity of a planet, star, or other massive celestial body, the concept of vertical is directly tied to the local gravitational field. When the gravitational field becomes extremely weak—either due to the small mass of the objects involved or their significant distance from the point of interest—the notion of vertical loses its practical meaning. In a simple, time-invariant, rotationally symmetric gravitational field, the vertical directions at different points in space intersect at the center of mass of the gravitational field. This means that no two distinct vertical directions are ever parallel to one another. A vertical direction will only be perpendicular to a horizontal plane if both are defined with respect to the same reference point. A plane is considered horizontal only at the specific point of reference. Consequently, both verticality and horizontality are inherently local concepts, and it is always necessary to specify the location to which the direction or plane refers. In reality, the gravitational field of a heterogeneous planet like Earth is deformed due to the uneven spatial distribution of materials with varying densities. As a result, actual vertical directions are neither straight lines nor necessarily convergent. At any given location, the total gravitational force is not constant over time because the objects generating the gravitational field move relative to one another. For example, on Earth, the local vertical direction at a specific point, as indicated by a plumb line, changes with the relative position of the Moon, which influences air, sea, and land tides. The difference between the gravitational force and the apparent weight of an object (as measured in a laboratory or in the field) arises from the centrifugal force associated with the planet's rotation. This centrifugal force is a fictitious force that only appears when calculations or experiments are conducted in non-inertial reference frames. The concept of a vertical line, while seemingly straightforward, is actually quite complex. In practice, most of the effects and variations associated with verticality are relatively small. They are measurable and can be predicted with high accuracy, but they generally do not significantly impact daily life. This apparent simplicity in everyday contexts contrasts with the scientific complexity of defining and measuring verticality, which arises because the scales relevant to daily life are several orders of magnitude smaller than the size of the Earth. Locally, the Earth appears flat, and vertical directions in nearby locations seem parallel. However, these are approximations, and their acceptability depends on the specific requirements of a given context or application, particularly in terms of accuracy. In graphical contexts, such as drawing or drafting on rectangular paper, it is common to associate one dimension of the paper with the vertical direction, even though the entire sheet of paper is positioned on a flat horizontal (or slanted) surface. In this case, the vertical direction is typically defined as extending from the side of the paper closest to the user to the opposite side farthest away. This convention, while seemingly natural when depicting a scene as it appears in reality, is purely arbitrary and can lead to misunderstandings or misconceptions, particularly in educational settings.
